9.1.b:
The bone cuts make the gaps (→ 08 TKA technique); this chapter makes them equal, so it starts with what "balanced" means.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you know a total knee is balanced?"
- "With trials in: **full motion**, **rectangular** equal gaps, stable to stress, patella tracking."
- "Answer both planes: **coronal** (medial vs lateral) and **sagittal** (flexion vs extension)."
- "Osteophytes off, cut first, then release the **concave, tight side** stepwise."

### Definition of a Balanced Knee
A balanced knee passes four tests, and all are judged with the trials in.

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Motion** | full range: 0–110/120° PS (posterior-stabilised), slightly less CR (cruciate-retaining) |
| **Gap shape** | **rectangular**: flexion = extension, medial = lateral |
| **Coronal stability** | negative varus–valgus stress test |
| **Patella** | normal tracking on a tilt or towel-clip test |

#### Trial Assessment
- Judge with **trials** and spacers, not cuts alone, because the construct shows real soft-tissue behaviour
- Put in the trials and a thin insert, release, then recheck at **90° and 45°** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- The trial and spacer photos are in 08 Trial Reduction
- Aim for **1–2 mm** of equal varus–valgus opening, rechecked after each release (Campbell)

#### After Cementing
- When the cement sets, put the trial insert in again
- Then check stability, motion, patellar tracking and the collaterals in flexion

### Clinical Significance
Balance is not a finishing touch; it decides how long the knee lasts.

#### Durability
- TKA (total knee arthroplasty) is "**a surgery of soft-tissue balancing**", its most important step
- A balanced knee shares the load between both condyles, so it lasts
- An unbalanced knee loads one side, so the polyethylene wears

#### Early Failure
- Any technique without balancing fails early, at about **3 months** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- A tight collateral or PCL (posterior cruciate ligament) gives **stiffness**
- A lax one gives **instability**, and then an early revision

#### Clinical Picture of Instability
- **Giving way**, recurrent effusion and diffuse peri-retinacular tenderness

### Coronal and Sagittal Balance
Balance has two planes, and each has its own rule.

#### Rectangle, Not Trapezoid
- **Rectangular** gaps in extension and flexion load medial and lateral equally
[[FIG: Fig 9.1 · 9.1
- A **trapezoidal** gap overloads the tight side, so the polyethylene wears and fails early
- **Condylar lift-off** under stress means eccentric load; test at 0°, 30°, 60° and 90°

#### Femoral Rotation and the Flexion Gap
- The flexion-gap shape also follows **femoral rotation**
[[FIG: Fig 9.2 · 9.1
- A femur cut parallel to the posterior condyles leaves a trapezoid; 3° of external rotation squares it
- An internally rotated femur makes the medial side tight and the lateral side loose

#### Varus and Valgus Deformity
- **Varus**: medial tight, lateral open. **Valgus**: lateral tight, medial open.
- The rule: release the **concave, tight** side, and fill the convex, stretched side with implant
- The cuts, square to the mechanical axis, have already corrected the bony deformity
- So the release grid treats only the soft-tissue imbalance left with the trials in

#### Correctable and Fixed Deformity
- Stress films show asymmetric opening
- A correctable deformity needs less release than a fixed one
- Long-standing valgus attenuates the **MCL** (medial collateral ligament), so it may fail after lateral release and need more constraint

#### Sagittal Plane
- The sagittal plane compares the flexion gap with the extension gap
[[FIG: Fig 9.3 · 9.1
- The details follow in 09.5

MEMORY HOOK — a brick, not a wedge
- The gap should be a brick, not a wedge: a wedge (trapezoid) crushes the polyethylene on its tight side.

### Intraoperative Assessment of the Gaps
Tools and the insert size tell you which gap is wrong, and whether bone or soft tissue is to blame.

#### Spacer Blocks
- **Spacer blocks** are company-specific
[[FIG: Fig 9.4 · 9.1
- J&J: a blue block for extension, and a motion block 1 mm smaller for flexion
- Using the blue block for both gaps is an error, so know your system

#### Laminar Spreaders
- **Laminar spreaders** show the gap shape before femoral rotation is set
- Use two, opposed; in osteoporotic bone, place them at the **rim**

#### Finger Test
- Under traction, put an index finger in each space
- Both sides tight means a bony cut problem; medial only means soft tissue

#### Timing of the Flexion-Gap Check
- Prof Shokry tests the flexion gap at 90°, after the chamfer cuts
- It can also be checked after the anterior and posterior cuts, before the chamfers
- Then the femoral size can still be changed

#### What the Insert Size Tells You
- If extension block **10** enters, the insert is usually 12; if **9**, usually 10
[[FIG: Fig 9.5 · 9.1

| Insert | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **10–12** | ideal: joint line restored |
| **9** | borderline: a cut or release problem |
| **14** | laxity |
| **17+** | one gap larger: poor cuts compensated by the insert |

- A **17 mm** insert needs an extra locking screw, so warn the company in advance (Prof Shokry)

#### Both Sides Tight
- If not even block 9 enters, it is a **cut error**
- So re-cut the bone, and never release both sides

### Mid-Flexion Instability
This is the angle most often missed, because surgeons test only at 0° and 90°.

#### Definition and Cause
- The knee is stable at 0° and 90° but lax near 45°, so the insert lifts forward
- A tight posterior capsule plus an extra distal cut raises the **joint line** >4 mm (Campbell)

#### Testing in Practice
- In a show of hands, only two attendees tested mid-flexion
- Case: the trial was unstable at 45°, so the insert went **12 → 17 mm** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- The **MCL** was plicated at 45° of flexion; the case film is in 15

### Preparation Before Release
Before any release, remove what fakes tightness, and cut first.

#### Osteophyte Removal
- Remove all **osteophytes** first, because they tent the capsule and collaterals
- Removal alone may balance the knee
- Releasing before removal gives false tightness, and so over-release

#### Posterior Osteophytes
- They stop flexion near 90° and tent the capsule, so a contracture follows
- The lateral film shows them (figure → 08 Finishing Cuts)
- Posterior femoral ones come out through the flexion gap, after the femoral cuts

#### Timing of Release
- No early release and no skeletonised tibia: cut first, then judge
- **Medial tibial overhang** tents the MCL and spoils the release, causing irritation and arthrofibrosis
- Release **stepwise** and recheck each step, because over-release cannot be undone without constraint

PITFALL — trapezoid flexion gap: ligament or rotation?
- An internally rotated femur makes the medial flexion gap tight and the lateral loose, mimicking a medial contracture
- Say → "**check femoral rotation first, then release the medial side in flexion**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Rectangle · 1–2 mm · test 45° · osteophytes first · concave side · both tight = bone**

9.2.b:
With the goal set, the next choice is how cuts and balancing are ordered: measured resection, gap balancing, or a hybrid.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "measured resection or gap balancing?"
- "**Measured**: cuts equal implant thickness, rotation from bony landmarks; for CR knees."
- "**Gap balancing**: tibia first, femoral rotation from the balanced flexion gap; for PCL-resected knees."
- "**Hybrid**: distal femur, tibia, balance extension, then finish the femur. Most surgeons do this."

### Sequence of the Operation
The order is fixed: exposure, cuts, balancing, implantation, closure.
- Cuts make the gaps, and balancing makes them equal
- Implanting before balanced trials locks the error in

### Measured Resection
The first strategy trusts the bone.

#### Principle
- Bone removed equals **component thickness**: 10 mm off for a 10 mm implant
[[FIG: Fig 9.6 · 9.2
- Soft tissue is ignored at this stage
- Rotation comes from bony **landmarks**; it was designed for **CR** knees, with the PCL intact
- With the PCL resected, true measured resection is hard, but current instruments allow it in PS knees

#### Advantages
- It keeps the joint line, **patellar tracking** and alignment, and it is reproducible

#### Disadvantages
- Landmarks are hard to palpate
- The **PCA** (posterior condylar axis) misleads in hypoplasia or valgus erosion
- The fixed 3° of external rotation is often not exact for that knee
- So the flexion gap comes out slightly wider medially or laterally

#### Late Releases
- Releases come after all the cuts, so the flexion gap may stay unbalanced
- That gives **lift-off** at 0–90° and eccentric polyethylene wear, so the lecturer dislikes it

### Gap Balancing
The second strategy trusts the ligaments.

#### Principle
- Soft tissue first: osteophytes off and contractures dealt with, or the gaps set rotation wrongly
- Then **tibia first**, and femoral rotation from a symmetric flexion gap
[[FIG: Fig 9.7 · 9.2
- So an extension gap of 15 mm means a flexion gap of 15 mm
- It ignores the TEA (transepicondylar axis) and Whiteside line; it suits **PCL-resected**, PS knees

#### Advantages
- The flexion gap is always **rectangular**, so no lift-off, no eccentric load and no loosening

#### Disadvantages
| Disadvantage | Why |
|---|---|
| **Joint line elevation** | a big deformity needs more resection, so relative baja |
| **Mid-flexion instability** | tight posterior capsule; tested at 0° and 90°, 45° forgotten |
| Non-anatomic rotation | landmarks ignored |
| Lost **posterior condylar offset** | big distal cut, then big posterior cut: less flexion, impingement |
| **Tibial error carried on** | a wrong tibial cut makes every femoral cut wrong |

- The tibial-cut reference needs a very well-balanced knee
- It is used mostly with the **LCS** mobile-bearing knee
- Femoral cuts go parallel to the tibia only after the extension soft tissues are balanced

### Hybrid Technique
Most surgeons take the best of both.

#### Principle
- Anatomic position plus balanced gaps: used by most surgeons and all current **instrument systems**
[[FIG: Fig 9.8 · 9.2
- Order: **distal femur**, tibia, balance the extension gap, finish the femur, then trials (Prof Sherif Khaled)

#### Rules
- Starting with the tibia or the distal femur are both fine
- Cutting the whole femur first turns it into measured resection, with the ligaments ignored
- Never finish the femur first: the extension gap is tested first, and removed bone is gone for good
- Beginners use measured resection; experienced surgeons use gaps (Prof Abdel Karim)

MEMORY HOOK — the map and the ropes
- Measured resection trusts the map (landmarks); gap balancing trusts the ropes (ligaments). The hybrid reads the map, then tests the ropes.

### Cutting Methods
The cuts can be guided by hand, computer or robot.
- Conventional, **navigation**, robotic, or PSI (patient-specific instrumentation: a 3D-printed block, not in Egypt)
- Navigation gives live alignment feedback, but a wrong **registration** makes everything wrong
[[FIG: Fig 9.9 · 9.2
- Navigation also measures the flexion and extension gaps through the whole range of motion
- Every implant has its own technique: request it, then do a demo and a **Sawbones** case first

### Alignment Philosophies
The last strategic choice is where to aim the limb.
[[FIG: Fig 9.10 · 9.2

#### The Five Philosophies
| Philosophy | Family (Rivière) | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical** (neutral) | systematic | tibia and femur cut at 90°, parallel: the most common |
| **Anatomic** (Hungerford, 1980s) | systematic | tibia at native 87°, femur parallel: line inclined 2–3° |
| **Adjusted mechanical** | hybrid | constitutional deformity kept, max 3° |
| **Restricted kinematic** | hybrid | big deformity corrected only to a safe zone (40° → 7–10°) |
| **Kinematic** | patient-specific (with UKA) | native alignment kept: needs a robot or navigation |

- Mechanical alignment is "systematic" because every knee gets the same cut
- Rivière's review is the only one that compares all of them

#### Why Each Was Introduced
- Anatomic left some knees in varus and was inconsistent; the 90° cut is not physiological
- Adjusted mechanical: patients were not used to a perfectly straight leg
- Restricted kinematic: a constitutional 20° may have become 40° with arthritis
- So kinematic would keep the arthritic 40°, and the restricted version stops at a safe zone

#### Kinematic Alignment
- A "true resurfacing": nothing is released, and the patient's own angle is kept
- So slight varus stays slight varus, and 1° of valgus stays 1°
- It cannot be done by eye with conventional jigs; most surgeons use a robot
- It claims faster recovery and better satisfaction, but this is **not proven** and not standard
- Critics: tibial varus outliers of ≥**4°** fail more often, so Campbell still recommends mechanical (Campbell)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Measured = landmarks, CR · gaps = tibia first, PS · hybrid = distal femur, tibia, then the rest**

9.3.b:
The varus knee is the common case, so coronal balancing starts on the tight medial side.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you release a varus knee?"
- "Release **medially**, off the tibia, stepwise."
- "Order: deep MCL, posteromedial corner, superficial MCL, then pes."
- "Posterior structures open **extension**; anterior ones open **flexion**."

### Anatomy of the Medial Sleeve
Each part of the sleeve is tight at a different angle, so first find the tight gap.
- The **posteromedial corner** is tight in extension; the **anterior superficial MCL** in flexion
[[FIG: Fig 9.11 · 9.3
- **Semimembranosus** has several posteromedial insertions
- With the POL (posterior oblique ligament), it forms the posteromedial corner

### Graded Medial Release
The Handbook grades the release by how many millimetres the medial side is tight.

| Medial tightness (Handbook) | Release |
|---|---|
| <2 mm | medial capsule + **deep MCL** |
| 2–4 mm | extension: posteromedial corner · flexion: anterior superficial MCL only |
| 4–6 mm | whole **superficial MCL**, posteromedial corner still spared |
| 6–8 mm | all the above |
| >8 mm | + **pes anserinus** (sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus) |

#### How Often and How Far
- A medial release is needed in nearly every varus primary
- Most stop at the first rung: osteophytes, periosteum and deep MCL
- Case: a stemmed varus knee needed no POL, semimembranosus or augment

#### Finding the Contracture
- If the block enters laterally only, there is a **medial contracture**
- Release and re-examine until medial equals lateral

#### Sequence at the Table
| Lecturer | Order of release |
|---|---|
| Prof Shokry | osteophytes · upper MCL + pes, subperiosteal · posterior deep MCL · posteromedial capsule |
| Prof Sherif Khaled | osteophytes · periosteal sleeve · posteromedial capsule + POL (cut or pie-crusted) · semimembranosus |

- Still tense: peel the capsular corner off bone, and the tibia externally rotates
- In his PS knees the PCL is resected in varus and valgus alike

### Release by Structure and Implant Design
Which structure to release depends on the tight gap and on the knee design.

#### Flexion or Extension Gap
- The anterior superficial MCL and pes open the **flexion** gap
- The posterior half, POL and semimembranosus open the **extension** gap

#### Posterior-Stabilised and Cruciate-Retaining Knees
- **PS**: the PCL, a secondary medial stabiliser, is resected first, so less release is needed
[[FIG: Fig 9.12 · 9.3
- So never release the whole sleeve in a PS knee
- **CR** with tight flexion: anterior superficial MCL and pes, then PCL, then posterior capsule

#### Whole Sleeve Released
- Still tight: advance the **LCL** (lateral collateral ligament) or add constraint

### Release Technique and Limits
The release is subperiosteal and gradual, with a bony option to spare the MCL.

#### Subperiosteal Release
- Work off the **tibia** with an elevator or osteotome, so the long MCL footprint lifts stepwise
- Lift the periosteum **2–3 cm**: the deep MCL is freed, the superficial MCL stays intact (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Lift the superficial MCL top-down, ≤**8 cm**, and never detach it completely (Prof Shokry)

#### Alternatives
- **Medial reduction osteotomy** ("shift resection" in the Handbook) spares the MCL
- Move the trial tray laterally while it stays flush, then resect the uncovered medial rim
- That slackens the medial sleeve; the tray is downsized or lateralised
- The Handbook also lists pie-crusting the superficial MCL
- Pie-crusting alone is not enough in varus, so the classic subperiosteal tibial release is used (→ 09.4)

MEMORY HOOK — peel the banana
- Peel the medial sleeve like a banana: top-down, **8 cm** at most, and never pull the skin off completely.

PITFALL — the over-released medial sleeve
- An over-released superficial MCL gives **flexion instability**, and a standard insert no longer holds
- Say → "**stepwise, recheck every step; an incompetent MCL needs a constrained condylar implant**"

The Handbook grades the release by how many millimetres the medial side is tight.

| Medial tightness (Handbook) | Release |
|---|---|
| <2 mm | medial capsule + **deep MCL** |
| 2–4 mm | extension: posteromedial corner · flexion: anterior superficial MCL only |
| 4–6 mm | whole **superficial MCL**, posteromedial corner still spared |
| 6–8 mm | all the above |
| >8 mm | + **pes anserinus** (sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus) |

#### How Often and How Far
- A medial release is needed in nearly every varus primary
- Most stop at the first rung: osteophytes, periosteum and deep MCL
- Case: a stemmed varus knee needed no POL, semimembranosus or augment

#### Finding the Contracture
- If the block enters laterally only, there is a **medial contracture**
- Release and re-examine until medial equals lateral

#### Sequence at the Table
| Lecturer | Order of release |
|---|---|
| Prof Shokry | osteophytes · upper MCL + pes, subperiosteal · posterior deep MCL · posteromedial capsule |
| Prof Sherif Khaled | osteophytes · periosteal sleeve · posteromedial capsule + POL (cut or pie-crusted) · semimembranosus |

- Still tense: peel the capsular corner off bone, and the tibia externally rotates
- In his PS knees the PCL is resected in varus and valgus alike

9.3.3.t: Release by Structure and Implant Design
9.3.3.b:
Which structure to release depends on the tight gap and on the knee design.

#### Flexion or Extension Gap
- The anterior superficial MCL and pes open the **flexion** gap
- The posterior half, POL and semimembranosus open the **extension** gap

#### Posterior-Stabilised and Cruciate-Retaining Knees
- **PS**: the PCL, a secondary medial stabiliser, is resected first, so less release is needed
[[FIG: Fig 9.12 · 9.3
- So never release the whole sleeve in a PS knee
- **CR** with tight flexion: anterior superficial MCL and pes, then PCL, then posterior capsule

#### Whole Sleeve Released
- Still tight: advance the **LCL** (lateral collateral ligament) or add constraint

9.3.4.b:
The release is subperiosteal and gradual, with a bony option to spare the MCL.

#### Subperiosteal Release
- Work off the **tibia** with an elevator or osteotome, so the long MCL footprint lifts stepwise
- Lift the periosteum **2–3 cm**: the deep MCL is freed, the superficial MCL stays intact (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Lift the superficial MCL top-down, ≤**8 cm**, and never detach it completely (Prof Shokry)

#### Alternatives
- **Medial reduction osteotomy** ("shift resection" in the Handbook) spares the MCL
- Move the trial tray laterally while it stays flush, then resect the uncovered medial rim
- That slackens the medial sleeve; the tray is downsized or lateralised
- The Handbook also lists pie-crusting the superficial MCL
- Pie-crusting alone is not enough in varus, so the classic subperiosteal tibial release is used (→ 09.4)

MEMORY HOOK — peel the banana
- Peel the medial sleeve like a banana: top-down, **8 cm** at most, and never pull the skin off completely.

PITFALL — the over-released medial sleeve
- An over-released superficial MCL gives **flexion instability**, and a standard insert no longer holds
- Say → "**stepwise, recheck every step; an incompetent MCL needs a constrained condylar implant**"

9.4.b:
The valgus knee mirrors the varus one: the tight side is lateral, and the releases come off the femur.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you release a valgus knee?"
- "Release **laterally**, off the femur."
- "**ITB** for extension, **popliteus** for flexion, LCL last."
- "Releases fix soft tissue only; a bony deformity needs a cut."

### Assessment of the Valgus Knee
Grade the deformity before choosing the release.
- Assess after the osteophytes and meniscus are out
- The **Ranawat** classification grades deformity size and MCL competence
- Releases fix soft tissue only, so a **bony deformity** needs a cut or osteotomy

#### Distal Cut on the Eroded Lateral Condyle
- Never deepen the distal cut to reach the worn lateral condyle, because it raises the joint line
- Leave the residual **2 mm** of lateral cartilage, then file or drill it (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- A later +2 mm recut removes it; never go beyond +2 mm

### Anatomy of the Lateral Side
The lateral structures crowd onto one small origin, so the release is precise.
- Release off the **femur**, sharply, because the LCL and popliteus share a small epicondylar origin
[[FIG: Fig 9.13 · 9.4
- The **popliteus** inserts anterior and distal to the LCL origin

### Release by Gap
As on the medial side, the tight gap picks the structure.

| Tight in | Release (Campbell, Miller) |
|---|---|
| **Extension** | **ITB** (iliotibial band): pie-crust, not transect · posterolateral capsule · posterior capsule off the femur |
| **Flexion** | **popliteus** |
| **Both** | **LCL**, last |
| Still tight in extension | lateral head of **gastrocnemius** |

- Structures are cut sharply off the femur; the ITB and posterior capsule are only pie-crusted

### Pie-Crusting
Pie-crusting lengthens a structure without cutting it through.
- Multiple **stab incisions**, by blade or needle, parallel to the joint line, lengthen taut fibres
[[FIG: Fig 9.14 · 9.4
- Lateral pie-crusting leaves a **tether**, so the lateral flexion gap opens little until the LCL is cut
- The **peroneal nerve** lies within **1.5 cm** of the posterolateral corner, so pie-crust with the knee **flexed** (Campbell)

### Order of Release
The order depends on the surgeon's school.

#### Schools
| Surgeon | First | Last |
|---|---|---|
| PS knee (Prof Sherif Khaled) | PCL out, pie-crust posterolateral capsule | ITB or popliteus |
| Sports surgeon | ITB | popliteus |
| Arthroplasty surgeon | popliteus | ITB |

#### Campbell's Advice
- Spare a slack popliteus
- For a small correction, release the posterolateral corner before the LCL
- Tight in extension only: pie-crust the ITB and check the **biceps** aponeurosis

#### The Handbook's Order
- Tight in flexion only: popliteus, then LCL, then the rest of the posterolateral corner
- Tight in both: release all four, the LCL, popliteus, posterior capsule and ITB

PITFALL — when does the LCL go?
- Campbell and Miller keep the LCL for "tight in both"; the Handbook cuts it second for flexion-only tightness
- Say → "**popliteus for flexion, ITB for extension, LCL last when both stay tight**"

### When Releases Are Not Enough
Some valgus knees stay unbalanced after a full release, and then constraint or advancement is needed.

#### Advancement and Constraint
- The PCL is often attenuated in valgus; if still unbalanced, inspect it, then consider **MCL advancement**
[[FIG: Fig 9.15 · 9.4
- A lateral flexion gap larger than extension can exceed the PS post **jump height**, so constrained condylar
- Elderly with a lax MCL: constrained condylar, but no routine **CCK** (constrained condylar knee), because 15° ≠ 50°

#### Severe Valgus
- In a 50° valgus, 8 mm off the medial distal femur leaves the lateral condyle ≈2 cm higher
- Never resect 2.5 cm of distal femur to meet it; make up the difference instead (Prof Sherif Khaled)

#### Peroneal Nerve
- Severe valgus with a contracture stretches the **peroneal nerve**
- For a palsy, flex the knee and loosen the dressings

MEMORY HOOK — shin or thigh
- Varus is released off the shin (tibia); valgus is released off the thigh (femur).

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Varus: tibia, deep MCL, POL, sMCL, pes · valgus: femur, ITB extension, popliteus flexion, LCL last**

9.5.t: Sagittal Balancing: Flexion and Extension Gaps
9.5.b:
Once medial equals lateral, the second plane asks whether flexion equals extension.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you balance the flexion and extension gaps?"
- "The **tibia** moves both gaps; the **distal femur** moves extension; the rest moves flexion."
- "**McPherson rule**: a symmetric problem, fix the tibia; an asymmetric one, fix the femur."
- "Tight: cut or release. Loose: add back with a thicker insert, bigger femur or augment."

### Principles
Each gap fails in a way the patient feels.
- A tight extension gap stops the knee straightening; a tight flexion gap stops it bending
- A loose gap is unstable
- A small difference is fine, and a slightly tighter flexion gap matters little

#### Loose Gaps in Practice
- **Recurvatum** is a loose extension gap
- A loose PS flexion gap lets the **cam jump**
- A little more tibia is harmless, but an over-wide flexion gap ends in flexion instability

### Determinants of Each Gap
To fix a gap, know what moves it.

| Gap | Controlled by (Miller) |
|---|---|
| **Both** | **tibial cut** · insert thickness |
| **Extension** only | **distal femoral cut** · posterior capsule, gastrocnemius |
| **Flexion** only | **posterior femoral cut** · femoral AP (anteroposterior) size · **PCL** in CR · tibial slope |

#### Femoral Size
- An undersized femur gives instability; an oversized one loses flexion
[[FIG: Fig 9.16 · 9.5
- Downsizing with **posterior referencing** notches the anterior femur, so use anterior referencing

#### Posterior Capsule
- Strip the **posterior capsule** after the femoral cuts, with a curved instrument, guarding the neurovascular bundle
[[FIG: Fig 9.17 · 9.5

### Posterior Cruciate Ligament in the Flexion Gap
In a CR knee, the PCL is the main soft-tissue lever on the flexion gap.

#### Effect and Signs
- PCL release opens the flexion gap **4–6 mm**, and the extension gap <2 mm (Campbell)
- A tight PCL makes the trial tray **lift off** in flexion
[[FIG: Fig 9.18 · 9.5
- At 90°, the PCL should deflect **1–2 mm** to pressure

#### Recession
- **Recession** is stepwise and subperiosteal, in 1–2 mm steps off the tibial bone island
- Retained PCL with tight flexion: snip, then recheck rollback
- In a PS knee, clear the PCL remnants

#### When the PCL Is the Wrong Lever
- If partial release fails, check the slope, or use a smaller femur with anterior referencing
- An incompetent PCL needs **PS** or deep-dish; >**75%** released needs more posterior constraint
- Slope outweighs a partial PCL release, and PCL release never corrects a **flexion contracture**

### McPherson Rule
One rule tells you which bone to touch.

#### The Rule
- A **symmetric** gap problem: adjust the **tibia**
- An **asymmetric** problem: adjust the **femur**
- The wrong bone makes two problems: the tibia for tight extension loosens flexion too

#### Applying the Rule
- The smallest block won't enter but flexion is fine: re-cut the **femur**
- Equal but too tight: more proximal tibia; equal but lax: a thicker insert

MEMORY HOOK — the floor and the walls
- The tibia is the shared floor of both gaps; the femur builds two separate walls.
- Same problem in both: fix the floor. Different problems: fix a wall.

### Gap Patterns
Two questions sort every case: which gap, and is it tight or loose?
[[FIG: Fig 9.19 · 9.5

| Extension ↓ / Flexion → | Tight flexion | Balanced flexion | Loose flexion |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tight extension** | cut more **tibia** | osteophytes + **posterior capsule**, then distal femur +2 mm | mixed (below) |
| **Balanced extension** | PCL/capsule, ↑ slope, then downsize femur or more posterior cut | balanced | **upsize femur** · posterior augment |
| **Loose extension** | mixed (below) | **distal femoral augment** | thicker **insert** · tibial augments |

### Tight Extension Gap
The danger here is taking too much distal femur.

#### How Much Bone
- Distal femur +**2 mm** only, then tibia, because repeated femoral recuts raise the joint line (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- The usual allowance is femur +2 mm and tibia +2–4 mm
- In a very tight knee, tibia +5–6 mm and femur +4 mm
- Move the distal jig, still on the pins left at "0", to the **+2 or +4** hole (Prof Shokry)
- The recut options drawing is in 08 Femoral Rotation

#### Flexion Deformity
- The hardest cases are short, small-built men with a **flexion deformity**
[[FIG: Fig 9.20 · 9.5
- **FFD** (fixed flexion deformity): extra distal femur, **2 mm** at a time (Campbell)
- Prof Sherif Khaled takes an extra **3 mm**, "as if the joint line rose 3 mm"
- Recurvatum: cut less distal femur, 7 vs 8–10 mm

PITFALL — how much distal femur for a contracture?
- Course: +2 mm, or 4 if very tight; for FFD +3 mm
- Campbell: max **4 mm** · Miller: 2 mm ≈ **10°**
- Say → "**capsule first, then distal femur 2 mm at a time, never past 4 mm**"

### Tight Flexion Gap
Here the order of steps protects the posterior offset.

#### Order of Steps
- Soft tissue first, then tibial **slope**, then posterior condyles last, so offset is kept (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- The Handbook goes bone first: more posterior cut, smaller femur, PCL recession in CR, slope last
- For the exam: PCL or capsule first in CR, and keep the posterior offset

#### Bone Steps
- A **4-in-1 block** on the +2 hole takes 2 mm more posterior condyle
[[FIG: Fig 9.21 · 9.5
- Downsizing changes AP only: cut the posterior condyles for the next size, with **anterior referencing** (Campbell)

### Loose Gaps
A loose gap is filled back, not cut.
- Loose flexion: **upsize the femur**, because the same size with a thicker insert spoils extension
- **Posterior augments** do the same, but often only on a **stemmed** femur
- Many companies make a stemmed femur only in revision systems, so read the manual first
- Loose extension: a distal augment, which also lowers a raised joint line

### Mixed Patterns
When one gap is tight and the other loose, there are two strategies.

| Pattern | Strategy 1: fix each gap at source | Strategy 2: loosen, then fill |
|---|---|---|
| Loose flexion + tight extension | distal cut or capsule + **upsize femur** | loosen extension, then thicker insert |
| Tight flexion + loose extension | posterior cut or downsize + **distal augment** | loosen flexion, then thicker insert |

#### Choosing a Strategy
- Strategy 1 keeps the **joint line**; Strategy 2 is simpler but may move it
- Upsizing risks mediolateral overhang and **patellofemoral overstuffing**
- A thick insert in an enlarged extension gap raises the joint line, so **pseudo-patella baja**

### Recurvatum
Recurvatum is a loose extension gap, and its cause decides the fix.

#### Correction Without Weakness
- Set the joint line **3–5 mm** distal and use a smaller femur, with anterior referencing (Campbell)
- So cut 2–3 mm less distal femur, and between sizes choose the smaller femur
- Ten patients corrected this way had no recurrence at 1 year

#### Neuromuscular Recurvatum
- Neuromuscular or quadriceps weakness makes it recur, so use a **hinge** with an extension stop

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Tibia both · distal femur extension · rest flexion · symmetric tibia, asymmetric femur**
